lesson.title: Seven Helices and a Molecular Switch: How GPCRs Run the Body's Most Common Signaling Pathway
lesson.summary: G protein-coupled receptors, built from a single polypeptide that spans the membrane seven times, detect an enormous range of signals and respond by activating an associated G protein that in turn controls enzymes such as adenylyl cyclase.
lesson.body:
G protein-coupled receptors, often abbreviated GPCRs, form the largest family of cell surface receptors, and their name describes both their structure and their mechanism. Structurally, a GPCR is a single polypeptide chain that weaves back and forth across the plasma membrane seven times, forming seven alpha helical transmembrane segments connected by loops, with the ligand binding region typically formed by the extracellular loops and the N-terminus. Mechanistically, the receptor's job once a ligand binds is to activate an associated G protein sitting on the cytoplasmic face of the membrane, which is where the family gets its name.

The G protein itself is a heterotrimeric complex of alpha, beta, and gamma subunits, and in its resting state the alpha subunit holds a molecule of GDP. When a ligand binds the GPCR and causes it to change shape, the receptor's cytoplasmic face acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, prompting the G protein's alpha subunit to release GDP and bind GTP instead. This GDP to GTP exchange is the actual switch: it causes the alpha subunit to separate from the beta gamma pair, and the GTP bound alpha subunit is now free to diffuse along the membrane and activate a target enzyme.

One of the best characterized targets is adenylyl cyclase, a membrane bound enzyme that, once activated by a GTP bound alpha subunit, converts ATP into the second messenger cyclic AMP. This is exactly what happens when the hormone epinephrine binds a beta adrenergic receptor, a GPCR found on liver, heart, and muscle cells: ligand binding activates a stimulatory G protein, which activates adenylyl cyclase, which raises cyclic AMP levels inside the cell, which in turn activates protein kinase A and sets off a phosphorylation cascade covered later in this chapter. Not every GPCR stimulates adenylyl cyclase this way; some couple to an inhibitory G protein that suppresses it instead, and others activate a different enzyme, phospholipase C, which generates the second messengers IP3 and diacylglycerol.

The GPCR system has a built in shutoff mechanism that keeps signaling transient rather than permanent. The alpha subunit itself has intrinsic GTPase activity, meaning it slowly hydrolyzes its own bound GTP back to GDP, which causes it to reassociate with the beta gamma pair and become inactive again. This self limiting property is essential. It means the strength and duration of a G protein's downstream effect depends on how quickly it deactivates itself, and mutations that slow this GTPase activity can lock the pathway in an abnormally active state, one mechanism by which certain toxins and tumors disrupt normal signaling.

GPCRs sit squarely within the cell surface receptor family introduced earlier: they are transmembrane proteins with an extracellular ligand binding surface and a cytoplasmic face that triggers transduction, they detect signals that cannot cross the membrane, and their activation is reversible and concentration dependent, just as basic ligand-receptor binding predicts. What makes them distinct is the specific intracellular partner they recruit, a heterotrimeric G protein, and the specific enzymes and second messengers that partner can switch on, a relationship explored in full detail in the sections on second messengers and cyclic AMP signaling.
